citation: Wilms, T., Wagner, P., Spawls, S., Beraduccii, J. & Malonza, P.K. 2021. Naja haje. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2021: e.T184071A1748178. Accessed on 15 May 2026.

actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species ranges from northern Western Sahara through the southern mountains of Morocco, northern Algeria, and central Tunisia to northern Libya and northern Egypt, south through through the Nile Valley at least as far south as Sennar in Sudan (Broadley 1994), including a large population at Lake Nasser (S. Baha El Din pers. comm.). South of the Sahara, it is found in the Sahel, Sudanian-Sahel, and Sudanian climatic zones of Niger and Nigeria east through Cameroon, Chad, eastern Sudan, and Torit in eastern South Sudan to Uganda and adjacent extreme western Kenya, with isolated records further east in the latter country (Samburo National Reserve, western Uaso Nyiro, and Lake Naivasha). There is an apparently separate subpopulation in north-central Tanzania and southern Kenya, with a northern range limit near Nairobi, and it may range into southern Tanzania (Spawls et al. 2002). In northeast Africa it also occurs in Ethiopia and Eritrea (Trape et al. 2009), and Djibouti (Ineich 2001); there are also records for northern Somalia (Trape et al. 2009). Its distribution in northeastern Africa is disjunct (Largen and Spawls 2010), and at least in Ethiopia this is thought to reflect its genuine distribution rather than being a sampling artefact (S. Spawls pers. comm. 2014), although Spawls et al. (2018) suggest that its apparently fragmentary range elsewhere may represent either local displacement by other snakes or a sampling artefact. Subpopulations of this snake appear to be sporadically distributed throughout much of its range, although it is possible that it has been overlooked in intervening areas (Spawls et al. 2002). In East Africa, it is found from 1,000 to 1,600 m asl (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.population: This cobra was formerly common in the Mediterranean region, but is now very rare. In Egypt it is an uncommon and declining species. It is reported to be rare by local people in Algeria (Trape et al. 2009), and is very rare in Djibouti (Ineich 2001). Animals can still be found reliably in East Africa outside heavily urbanized areas, and persist even in well-populated areas of Ethiopia, but in low numbers (S. Spawls and P. Malonza pers. comm. 2014). As a large, venomous snake that is known to prey on chickens, it is subject to persecution and won't persist in heavily-populated areas, but is probably not undergoing more than local declines in East Africa (S. Spawls pers. comm. 2014).
documentation.habitats: This terrestrial cobra is found in areas with grassy vegetation, thorny scrub and occasionally in water. It occurs in semi-desert, but it is not a desert species. Habitats include steppe, grassland, dry savanna, semi-desert, oases, wadis, traditional agricultural areas, stone walls, ditches, gardens and buildings. It may occur in woodland, but is never found in forest (Spawls et al. 2002). In Ethiopia it is found in heavily degraded acacia woodland, from which other cobras are typically excluded (S. Spawls pers. comm. 2018). Animals eat frogs, toads, eggs, small mammals and snakes (Spawls et al. 2002), as well as chickens. The female lays between eight and 33 eggs.
documentation.threats: Large numbers of animals are caught for use in local markets by snake-charmers in Egypt, and it is directly persecuted in parts of its range. Animals may be sold as curios to tourists. Large numbers are collected in Egypt for venom extraction for the development of serum, and these animals are generally not returned to the wild. In Egypt the snake is threatened by habitat loss through overgrazing and large-scale land reclamation projects. As a snake which feeds predominantly on rodents, it may also be locally subject to accidental poisoning caused by the use of rodenticides. Urbanization, and the persecution that results from increased human densities, are the major threats in East Africa, and probably also in Ethiopia (S. Spawls pers. comm. 2014), but are localized (P. Malonza and S. Spawls pers. comm. 2014).
documentation.measures: This snake occurs in some protected areas. The development of sustainable harvesting for this species is needed in Egypt. Further taxonomic work is needed to establish if North African subpopulations are distinct from those elsewhere in the species' range (S. Baha El Din pers. comm.).
documentation.use_trade: This snake is used by snake-charmers and is collected to create curios for tourists. Large numbers are taken into captivity for venom extraction. While the snake is of interest for display in zoos, there is limited demand for this animal in the international pet trade. Jensen et al. (2019) reported 84 animals advertised for export from Egypt and Tanzania between 2013 and 2017.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern on the basis that this species is widespread, highly adaptable, and likely to be subject to only localized threats from collection, habitat degradation and pesticide use. Declines across much of the north of this species' range may warrant specific conservation actions in these areas, particularly in Egypt.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Records from west of Niger represent Naja senegalensis, formerly confused with this species (Trape et al. 2009). North African populations may also be taxonomically distinct, and further research is needed to clarify the systematics of this species (S. Baha El Din pers. comm.).
